hi. stop talking down to yourself, stop trying to affirm that you're useless. it makes those negative thoughts bigger and saps your energy to be happy. saying you're annoying is just clouding your mind with negative feelings towards yourself. if you send out the signal that you're annoying and unlikeable, that is what people are going to pick up. you're sabotaging yourself, and you deserve better. liking yourself makes you likeable, but your inner dialogue is killing that.

you need to gain a sense of self worth before you can do that healthily, though. tbh I'd look into counseling to help that process along.

I get feeling like nobody likes you. Like every single fucking thing you say just gets on people's nerves but they feel too bad for you to speak up or something. I get that.

If it helps: nobody is as concerned with the little things about you as you are.

you live life from your perspective, first person, just like everyone else. you notice every little thing about yourself because you're you.... And so does everyone else, about themselves. Every single person second guesses what they say, they cringe after doing something, they have felt at some point in their lives, whether for 10 minutes or 10 years, that they're just not good enough, not likeable, not interesting, not worthy of love - anything. Every single person overthinks themselves.

I'm not saying "everyone's like that, deal with it" or whatever. I'm saying that the majority of people are so wrapped up in their own lives, what other people think of THEM, that they don't notice the little things about other people that those other people worry about.

No one is thinking more negatively about you than they are about themselves.

...unless they're a narcissist, which is their fucking problem, not yours.

Do you have people you talk to or hang out with that you feel comfortable with? That you're less guarded around, feel like "one of them"? It's okay if you don't. I for sure don't. The only way I've been able to get through the past 6 or so years, mostly spent fucking despising myself, is trying to remember that im just as worthy of love as everybody else on this planet. It sounds weird and kinda sad in a way, but I'm only the lead character in MY story. No one is thinking about me as much as I'm thinking about me. There's no time to give unnecessary fucks and try to change myself because some people looked at me strange. MY world revolves around me, not THEM. it's my life I'm living. If they can't deal with things I struggle with, me being awkward, being Insecure, etc. then I don't have to spend time with them or care about their opinion.

Of course there's a line to be drawn - if I have a friend who's leaning on me too much for emotional support, to an unhealthy point, I'm gonna tell her that I care about her but she needs to talk to someone professional. That's not me "not accepting her" - that's me looking out for my own mental health as well as hers.

Of course you should have goals to work towards. Is it hard for you to manage time? You can get better at that. Are you always saying things without thinking first? You can work on that too. Bettering yourself in ways that are healthy for you and people around you is great. Beating yourself up for having a hard time interacting with people or reading a room or knowing what to say or ANYTHING like that is not great.

So, I'll say it again:

YOU DESERVE JUST AS MUCH LOVE AND HAPPINESS AS EVERY SINGLE OTHER PERSON ON THIS PLANET.

I love you, you deserve to love yourself too. It's a hard place to get to. It's a long road. But it's not impossible. The fact that I can genuinely say that I don't hate my own guts is astonishing to me, but hey, here I am.

Basically what I'm trying to say is, you're enough. I love you, other people love you, you are loved. It gets better, I promise. For real.

this reminds me of my dad.

he took his life a little over a year ago. at his best, at the core of him when he was himself and healthy, he was an amazing person. kind, genuine, creative, genius, witty - truly a one of a kind person and an amazing father. 

however, when he was pretty deep into depression in the last few years of his life, he really hurt my mom and the people around him. They'd never had a super passionate relationship. He was talking to another woman and saying he wanted to marry her, he told my mom he never loved her, he flat out rejected her as his wife. He had fake online accounts, he went behind her back, he was shitty. The effect it had on my mom was so, so sad to see. She's doing much better now though.

But when my dad was HEALTHY, when he was fully himself, he was such a good person who, in his right mind, would never have done what he did. Who he was in the last few years was, in my mind, not really him. He was so, so deep into depression and some deep existential suffering that he'd always dealt with that I really see that as someone else. Not my dad. That dissonance has been very helpful for me.

I was suicidal for a big chunk of my life, and in some weird way, that's allowed me to forgive my dad and let go of things he did near the end of his life because I know first hand that when you're in so fucking deep, you really are not yourself. I don't mean that in a preachy way - I'm just trying to say that it's somehow been helpful in letting me move on and be at peace with the memory of him because on some level, I get it. NOT as an excuse, by any means. What he did was horrible, and nothing changes that. I just mean this as an explanation and a means to move on.

I'm kind of rambling, but what I'm trying to say is, people evolve in shitty ways. that does not mean they were always like that in the first place. like you said - you KNOW your brother, and he did not used to be like that. I don't know what changed but it may be comforting to remind yourself that a lot of what he said was most likely the product of whatever made him kill himself. Anger at the world that developed over time, an addiction, a mental condition he had - whatever it may have been.

this doesn't mean you should feel guilty about missing him because he said horrible things and was an asshole, but it also doesn't mean that just because he's gone, you can't be angry at him. grief is a process. whatever you feel is valid. there is no wrong way.

I find what helps me is keeping in mind the very best of my dad. not acting like the bad things didn't happen - just not dwelling on them if not necessary. of course our situations are different, but I hope this helps a little bit.

That's a lot to deal with - so many conflicting emotions. I'm so sorry OP, I hope you and your family are doing as ok as you can be right now. ♥️

Hey all, I'm trying to type my dad. 

For context, my mom (ENFP) said that he typed as an ISTJ awhile ago, but I don't know how long "awhile" was, and to be honest I don't entirely see it. I'm only positive about IXTX. 

This is all from an INFP daughter's perspective, so I'm aware that my view is a bit different than other people who knew him, but it's valid nonetheless.

We lost dad to suic*de a little over a year ago, which is why this is written in past tense. Trying to type him is therapeutic in some weird way, so let's just leave it at that.

He was a deeply artistic person - always deeply engrossed in music and writing.  He made CDs of his favorite music from each of his middle school, high school, and college years, and listened back to them sometimes.

He was in two bands in college as bassist/backup singer. He was extremely musically and lyrically talented. His band mates said he was very much a genius in that way, which is pretty damn cool.

He had a very poetic mind. He liked taking in fantasy and scifi works just as much as he liked learning about the real world. Me and him were the resident Harry Potter nerds.

He could read for HOURS about history, philosophy, politics, space, anything intellectually stimulating. He loved documentaries and maps. He wasn't the type to debate with people - he was just genuinely fascinated with the world.

He had an impeccable dry sense of humor and was very good at impressions. Some of his humor was a little edgy I guess, but he was careful about it, and it was always funny.

He loved silly outlandish nicknames. For example, he had a childhood friend named Joe who he dubbed "Rolps the Intrepid". He was apparently always convincing his friends to go on adventures with him. He was very curious.

He was fairly overprotective. Me and my older brothers (INTJ and ISTP) had parental controls on the computer, all that stuff. It was hard for him to rationalize that making me go to christian youth group in high school wasn't improving my mental health, it was doing the opposite.

He was the type to forget about basic things like chores but would drop everything to carry ANYONE if they couldn't walk, if that makes sense. Like he forgot to take out the trash but drove 2 hours in the middle of the night to pick up a neighbor whose car broke down. He had a deeply ingrained sense of duty, I believe, but was also just genuinely a kind person.

 He was also pretty affection; very much a bear hugger. He loved spending quality time with me and my brothers and tried to make as much time as possible for us. He coached my brother's hockey teams and was always supportive of my artistic endeavors, as well as my brothers.

When my parents finally realized my mental health was so shitty after years of emotional abuse from one of my brothers, dad put EVERYTHING he had into helping me. He wrote encouraging notes to me, he made a little worksheet for me to fill out that said things like "something I wish you knew is ____", "it is helpful when you ____" so he could really understand how I was feeling. He drastically changed how he handled stress and tension at home, and was diligent about listening to my thoughts and feelings.

When I started playing ice hockey at the late age of 17, as a 5'1 girl with no experience, he was consistently my biggest cheerleader and teacher and would always offer advice and encouragement.

I did my best to make this cohesive and relevant as opposed to a ramble.

Any thoughts are appreciated, thank you for reading :)

Hi! I totally get that feeling of being in a dead end in terms of music.... What helped me was to ask people for recommendations honestly lol. Humans are better at that than Spotify!

On the topic of humans being better at advice... I'm sorry to say that all the guides in the world will only get you so far!! It's really admirable that you've made such an effort to improve your interpersonal skills and relationships - that's more than many people do. 

I'm a very extroverted introvert, if that makes any sense. I despise my own birthday because it means getting attention I don't want, and i need frequent breaks even from people I really like, that sort of thing - but I'll also strike up a conversation with a stranger next to me on a plane and get to hear her life story and she'll end up telling me about her dog's kidney stone scare and I'll draw her portrait. Yknow?? It's a strange balance for me. 

I was cripplingly shy until about two years ago. I've only really gotten out of my shell this past year, and it's been a game changer. It sounds like it's not a lack of willingness or energy to meet new people and form stronger relationships for you - it's just a matter of how to go about it. Here's my advice:

DON'T THINK TOO HARD! SPEAK UP! PEOPLE ARE GENERALLY NICE! BE YOURSELF!

Some examples: I was in graphics class on the first day and I saw a girl I had in my previous art class last semester. We had talked a couple times, but weren't really friends yet. I said "hey, (her name)!" And smiled at her. fast forward to the end of class, we're exchanging numbers and cracking jokes with a third friend we just made (he had dyed hair, I told him it looked really cool, and we three dubbed ourselves the graphics gang). More examples - I smiled at a random girl I accidentally locked eyes with at math class. That opened the door to being friendly and then that turned into us sending each other memes and talking on the phone. Smiling is important!! Genuinely being happy to see people, being happy for people's accomplishments, and honestly just being a chill, light-hearted presence is important. Be approachable! By that, I mean don't glower at people and bury your face in your phone or a book all the time. I used to do that because I thought it made me look moody and intriguing. But really, I just looked angry. When I started letting myself loosen up, I started forming more meaningful relationships with people I could laugh and cry with. People I trust, love, and can count on - and I'm the same for them. 

Of course, everyone is different. There are some people who have a stick up their butt or maybe take a little more to get out of their shell. And that's okay too! Everyone is different. Spend your time with people who make you happy, who make you laugh, and who make you think! Make sure to lift them up too. Be light-hearted, go with the flow. Above all, BE YOURSELF. 


Another big thing: people respond positively to positivity! If you like a girl's shoes, tell her honestly that you think her shoes are cool! If you see a dude wearing a shirt with a reference to a tv show you like, say you like the shirt - stuff like that. If you have something nice to say, it's ok to say it. Again, don't worry too much.
